newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian Senate gives green light to reform push.
newsitem.headline: Italian Senate gives green light to reform push.

text.p: Italy's Senate voted overwhelmingly on Thursday to set up a special commission of both houses of parliament to draft reforms to the country's outdated and inefficient institutions.

The upper house vote for the bicameral commission on constitutional reform was 256 to 16 with two abstentions after the centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance joined centre-left government coalition senators in backing the plan.
It now goes to the lower Chamber of Deputies for a similar vote next week. Both houses approved the proposal on a first reading last year.

The 70-member commission will have just five months to propose overhauls to the powers and structure of government and parliament and a blueprint for federal reform. Recommendations will go to parliament and finally to a referendum.
The framework laid down in Italy's 1948 constitution now is widely considered incapable of ensuring effective and durable government and efficient parliamentary law-making.

The clamour for change has grown in the wake of corruption scandals that topped the old political class, but deep differences divide parties in the centre-left government and the opposition on how to remodel the state.

The Freedom Alliance agreed to support the proposed commission on Tuesday only after leader Silvio Berlusconi prevailed over his hard-right ally Gianfranco Fini, who had wanted reform tackled by a specially elected assembly.
Fini until this week had argued for a "no' vote by the opposition in order to deny the plan the two-thirds majority needed to avoid putting it to a referendum.

He told Italian television on Wednesday night that the row over the process had almost torn apart the Freedom Alliance, which governed briefly in a stormy coalition with the separatist Northern League in 1994.
Social democrat leader Massimo D'Alema and Berlusconi have been the most enthusiastic supporters of the commission.
Their respective parties, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) and Forza Italia, are the biggest in parliament and have the most to gain from change.
Speakers on both sides of the political divide, however, made clear that change could only come about if all parties agreed not to make the commission a political battleground.
"The challenge facing us is difficult but not impossible," Cesare Salvi, the PDS leader in the Senate, said.
"We can all win as long as the bicameral commission does not become a playing field which people will leave as winners and losers after a battle waged with slogans...and abstract formulas," he said.

The main fight is expected to be over the powers of government, with the centre-right pushing for direct election of the prime minister to replace the existing system under which the premier is appointed by the president.
The centre-left opposes the proposal, arguing that it would invest one person with too much power.

More common ground has been evident between the two main blocs on the need to change the unwieldy structure of parliament, whose two chambers duplicate each other's functions and thus slow down law-making, and on federal reform.
The League, which is pushing for secession for the affluent north, voted against the commission.
